title: The Burton Trial
note: Salt Lake Herald, February 21 – March 6, 1879. “The Burton Trial,” daily reports of Burton’s trial for the murder of Isabella Bowman. The fullest account in the free archives. Former Morrisites testified for the prosecution and gave their homes in 1879. Among them were James Bowman (of Soda Springs since 1863), Mrs. Mary Anderson (of Soda Springs), Caroline Eliason, Mrs. Emma Just (of the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho), Jacob Johnson, Thomas Williams (of Ogden since 1865), Philip Hewitt (Salt Lake City) and a man from Hyrum whose name the scan garbles. Men of the posse also took the stand, among them Christopher Sproat, William H. Hunt and Dan Camomile. The defense called Thomas Abbott of Farmington, Robert W. Burton of Kaysville, John C. Thompson of Riverdale and Burton himself. Abraham Taylor, one of the seven convicted in 1863, testified near the close (reported March 4). The Ogden Junction of February 22 names another prosecution witness, Joseph Warner, born in Germany, who told the court of a vision of Joseph Smith at Providence that had got him cut off from the Latter-day Saint church, read a sermon of his own and recited a revelation. The text of these scans is poor, and the names are as read from it. title: Railroad Meeting at Gwendale
note: New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2. “Railroad Meeting at Gwendale.” Also June 18, 1875, p. 3; September 8, 1876, p. 3; July 6, 1877, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3; April 30, 1880, p. 4; January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3; May 4, 1883, p. 3. Notices that place Gwendale, later Morristown, in the upper Deer Lodge valley. The April 1875 mass meeting of “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” at the Gwendale school house was chaired by Morgan Evans, with W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee. Primaries were held at Wier’s store (1875); the 1876 election judges for Gwendale were Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen and Wm Wier; a W W Thomas of Gwendale paid a subscription (1877); and a fifty-ton smelter at Gwendale began work in August 1877. A land-office notice of March 1880 lists Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims awaited a hearing on whether the land was mineral, among them Daniel James, William P. Thomas, Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen. In January 1882 John R. Eardley built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and in March he was appointed postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was.” By 1883 school district No. 6 was called Willow Glen. None of these items calls anyone a Morrisite. title: [Untitled item], New North-West
note: New North-West, September 3, 1886, p. 3. Also February 19 and March 26, 1886, p. 3. “A Mormon Church, of the Morrisite branch, we are informed, is being constructed under the superintendence of Elder Clapp on the Cottonwood road about a half mile east of town.” An Elder J. C. Clapp had preached at the Deer Lodge court house in February and March 1886, once on the “Origin of the American Indians,” a Book of Mormon theme. The Morrisites’ own minutes settle the question: in November 1886 their council recorded an invitation from “Elder Clapp of the Reorganized Church” to use that church’s meeting house at Deer Lodge City while he was preaching in Utah (Church History Library, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 37–38). The building was the Reorganized Church’s, not a Morrisite church; Clapp was very probably the RLDS missionary Joseph C. Clapp. Other links: Chronicling America: https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn84038125/1886-02-19/ed-1/?sp=3; Chronicling America: https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn84038125/1886-03-26/ed-1/?sp=3 Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: Charity for the Mormons
note: Salt Lake Tribune, May 31 to July 5, 1891. “Charity for the Mormons,” letters 1–6 of “The Elder”: May 31, p. 10 (“Charity for the Mormons”); June 7, p. 16 (“Church of God and Kingdom of God”); June 14, p. 17 (“The Apostles Ancient and Modern”); June 21, p. 3 (“The Priesthood Mistake”); June 28, p. 20 (“A Church That Is Fallen”); July 5, p. 3 (“Are the Mormons Sincere?”). The first six letters, on the Latter-day Saint church: the first is signed “an Elder of the Old-time Church, and a friend to the Mormon people,” and calls 1891 “a year of expectancy of great things.” The second argues that the kingdom of God is yet to come (the letter John R. Eardley described as Parson’s, on “the difference existing between a church and a kingdom”). The third calls Joseph Morris “a reforming prophet,” “one of the most innocent, meek, and inoffensive men that ever lived,” who went to Brigham Young and each of the apostles. The fourth teaches priesthood by birthright, to be shown by a prophet with the Urim and Thummim. The sixth urges that Joseph Smith III be invited to lead a united church and says the first Morrisites were cut off for refusing to testify that Brigham Young was a prophet. title: Massacre of Morrisites. The Inside History of That Dreadful Deed
note: Salt Lake Tribune, July 26, 1891, p. 3. “Massacre of Morrisites. The Inside History of That Dreadful Deed.” The ninth letter. Letter 9. Parson’s surrender to Judson Stoddard, the deaths of Morris, Banks and two women, the eleven Morrisite dead, and the seven sentenced and pardoned (the list does not agree with the court report). Also where some survivors went: Soda Springs, Reese River and Carson Valley, where the writer knew “Bishop Cook, Parson, Eardly and many others.” Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Other links: Newspapers.com: https://www.newspapers.com/image/12202725/ Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: The Morrisite Tragedy: A Thrilling Incident in the History of Mormonism
note: Anaconda Standard, July 26, 1891, p. 11. “The Morrisite Tragedy: A Thrilling Incident in the History of Mormonism.” An unsigned account sympathetic to the Morrisites, from Morris’s arrival at South Weber through the surrender. It appeared the same day as the Tribune’s ninth letter, but the text differs. Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: The Morrisite History
note: Salt Lake Tribune, July 30, 1891, p. 4. “The Morrisite History.” An editorial praising the letters of “The Elder” as “a full, true, and calm history of the Morrisite movement,” written by “a sincere and pious man” who believed in the church “as it was first organized.” It does not name him. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: Local News
note: Salt Lake Herald, July 31, 1891, p. 4. “Local News.” The Herald’s reply: the Tribune’s Morrisite history is “a bungling falsehood,” printed to win votes for disfranchising the Mormons. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: What Is Mormonism Now?
note: Salt Lake Tribune, August 2, 1891, p. 3. “What Is Mormonism Now?” Letter 10 of “The Elder.” The last letter of the series, on the failure to build the temple in Jackson County. No Morrisite content. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

note: San Francisco Chronicle, June 19, 1892. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: On Trial for His Reason
note: Salt Lake Herald (semi-weekly), Friday, March 11, 1904. “On Trial for His Reason.” Also Salt Lake Telegram, March 9, 1904, “Alleged to Be Insane.” William Jones of Blaine, Davis County, in his eightieth year, called the man “who caused the Morrisite War,” faces his daughters’ petition for a guardian (Second District Court, probate division, sitting at Ogden); the report recalls that he was held prisoner by the Morrisites, escaped and came back with the militia, and was a witness for the defense at Burton’s trial. The Telegram (p. 10) and the daily Herald (p. 1) carry the same report on March 9, 1904; the Telegram and gives his age as 80, which fits William J. Jones of the roll, born in 1825. The Herald clipping shows only “Friday, Mar[ch]” and the dateline “Ogden, March 8”; its date is the next Friday. Herald clipping at South Weber City. Other links: daily Herald, March 9, p. 1: https://newspapers.lib.utah.edu/details?id=12207568 Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1901

title: Morrisite Murders. The Case for the Mormons
note: Truth (Brisbane, Australia), May 5, 1907, p. 2. “Morrisite Murders. The Case for the Mormons.” Letter of J. F. Nash. A Latter-day Saint’s reply to the paper’s article “Murdered Morrisites,” which drew on Fanny Stenhouse. Nash dates that article April 14, 1907 (the NZ reprint of his letter says April 11); it has not been found on Trove. The exchange between Nash and J. W. Barkus of Coorparoo ran in Brisbane Truth through the summer, and John Norton’s Truth in Wellington reprinted it. Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Other links: Newspapers.com: https://www.newspapers.com/image/1026593890/ Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1901

title: Helped Establish Fort Douglas
note: Salt Lake Tribune, February 18, 1907, p. 2. “Helped Establish Fort Douglas.” Interview with Presto Burrell, a sergeant in Connor’s command. He recalls the Morrisite men in the penitentiary in the winter of 1862–63 and their pardon, and says his company escorted the Morrisite colony to Soda Springs in the spring of 1863. He later took up a ranch on the Blackfoot River. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1901

title: Gen. Burton’s Death

title: [Untitled item], Silver State Post
note: Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), January 15, 1954, p. 2. A feature on George Johnson, then 97. Johnson’s own story as the paper told it: born near Copenhagen in 1856, he came to Council Bluffs at fifteen, became a Morrisite minister, crossed to Montana by wagon train with Andrew Hendrickson, reaching it “early in 1874,” and preached in family homes as Hendrickson’s assistant before he was ordained and the two led in building the church. His obituary and a 1956 article give 1873 for the journey. Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1954

title: George Johnson Sr’s Last Rites Sunday, Burial in Hillcrest
note: Silver State Post (Deer Lodge, Mont.), May 7, 1954, p. 7. “George Johnson Sr’s Last Rites Sunday, Burial in Hillcrest.” Johnson died on the morning of Thursday, April 29, 1954, at ninety-eight. An Episcopal priest conducted the funeral, quoting the words Johnson had used at funerals “as a minister of the Morrisite faith,” and he was buried in Hillcrest cemetery beside his wife, who died in 1907. The paper calls the Morrisite church “almost extinct these days.” Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1954

title: Karl Banks Speaks to Mothers Study Club January 22
note: Pleasant Grove Review, January 30, 1958, p. 4. “Karl Banks Speaks to Mothers Study Club January 22.” Karl Banks of Pleasant Grove, grandson of John Banks, on Banks and Morris. He gave the talk again to other groups (the “Mormon Forum” at Gordon Howard’s home in Bountiful, with Juanita Brooks, Review, June 29, 1961; a DUP camp, April 20, 1972), and in 1968 read a manuscript of his on the siege to a Utah history study group at his home (Review, October 31, 1968). Its retelling has errors of date. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

note: Salt Lake Tribune, March 3, 1974, p. 68. Review of Agnes Just Reid, Letters of Long Ago (Tanner Trust edition). Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

note: Standard-Examiner (Ogden), May 30, 1974, p. 17. On Mark Stuart’s collection of Uintah artifacts. note: Ogden Standard-Examiner, June 29, 1975, p. 22B. “Morrisite War Touche[d] …” (headline only partly read). An anniversary retelling. Newspapers.com links need a subscription. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

note: Davis County Clipper, October 22, 1976, p. 34. “Historians Honor Dr. Howard.” Gordon M. Howard of Bountiful receives the Utah State Historical Society’s Dale L. title: [Untitled item], Standard-Examiner
note: Standard-Examiner (Ogden), May 9, 1979, p. 75. Debbie Boothe, on the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery. Says Joseph Werner lay in an unmarked pauper’s grave. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: [Untitled item], Davis News Journal
note: Davis News Journal, April 3, 1980, p. 9. Doneta Gatherum, South Weber column. After the war the fort’s land was taken up by neighbors: a school on the southwest, John Firth on the northeast, John Bowman’s rock house (1875) on the southeast, Parley Prophet on the northwest, and the center (about 475 East 6650 South) a town square and ball field. Its dates for the siege are wrong. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: [Untitled item], Davis News Journal
note: Davis News Journal, May 29, 1980, p. 15. Doneta Gatherum, on the Parley Prophet home. Parley Prophet’s first log house stood just west of the old Morrisite fort; his grandson Glen Ray recalls the fort area as the town park, with home plate near the house’s east windows, which had to be shuttered. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: South Weber School
note: Davis News Journal, October 16, 1980, p. 25. Doneta Gatherum, “South Weber School.” The South Weber schoolhouses of 1859 (adobe), the second and the 1888 frame school stood just inside the old fort, about 440 East 6650 South; with Glen Ray’s and Leonard Bowman’s recollections and a drawing of the 1888 school by Charles Lunn. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: [Untitled item], Davis News Journal

title: Prime Time
note: Daily Herald (Provo), July 19, 1981, p. 50. Theron H. Luke, “Prime Time” column. On Connor’s escort of the Morrisites to Soda Springs and Morristown; counts at least six Morrisites killed, four of them women, and two militiamen; describes the Anderson monument in the Soda Springs cemetery. note: Salt Lake Tribune, April 28, 1983, p. 75. On Leonard Bowman and South Weber. Bowman says he learned about 1981 where Werner was buried and had a marker made for him, and that Werner lived in a tent in the village square. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

note: Lakeside Review (North Edition), May 23, 1984, p. 2. On the South Weber Pioneer Cemetery. Gives the marker’s wording, “Joseph Werner Morrisite, died about 1870,” and says Mattie Ray had placed five new headstones. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: South Weber History Dates Back to 1851
note: Lakeside Review, October 30, 1985, p. 28. “South Weber History Dates Back to 1851.” Drawn from the DUP’s East of Antelope Island and other writings. Retells the siege, including the cannonball that landed in the lap of William J. Jones’s mother, “in the possession of Alberta Peek” (see Kington Fort). Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: John Bear: Mission to Providence
note: Herald Journal (Logan), May 15, 1988, p. 47. “John Bear: Mission to Providence.” John Lebrecht Bear, a Swiss convert at Providence, Cache Valley, left for Kington Fort about August 15, 1861, with at least four other Providence families; his wife and child were killed by the posse’s cannon in June 1862. He went to Soda Springs, married a fellow Morrisite there in 1863, and later joined the Reorganized Church. Drawn in part from his unpublished autobiography. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: From Morrisites to Marcus Daly
note: Montana Standard (Butte), July 2, 1989, pp. 69–71. Roger Kelley, “From Morrisites to Marcus Daly.” An interview with the Anaconda historian Alice Finnegan. She calls the Morrisites the area’s first settlers, says they wintered at Gregson (now Fairmont Hot Springs) before homesteading, and names Morgan Evans, who bought the land for Daly’s town and smelter, as a Morrisite. Morris’s Anaconda, Montana (1997) describes Evans’s arrival in 1866 without calling him one, and he is not on the 1861–62 roll; the claim is unconfirmed. Brought to this guide’s attention by Jim and Barbara Furshong. Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: Farmington Cannon Stays despite Claim
note: Standard-Examiner (Ogden), September 11, 1989, p. 15. Valerie Phillips (Lakeside Review), “Farmington Cannon Stays despite Claim.” The Daughters of Utah Pioneers’ 1947 marker by the old cannon at Farmington says it was used at Nauvoo, brought west in 1847 and used in the “Morrisite battle at Uintah in 1862.” The cannon collector James H. Ambrose of Vernal identified it as a Civil War gun cast by the Joseph Reid Anderson company of Richmond, Virginia, in 1864, so it cannot have been at the siege. The Anderson family also took it for the gun that wounded Mary Christoffersen Anderson (Peter Anderson, Frontier Times, June–July 1965, p. 48). Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1951

title: [Untitled item], Standard-Examiner
